traveler: Saint Denis of Paris (Dionysius, Denys), first bishop of the Parisii
title: The Head Carried North: Denis of Paris, the Hill of Mercury, and the Abbey of the Kings
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Heliopolis, the sun goes dark out of season
stops.date_confidence: legendary. The Golden Legend opens Denis's life in Egypt and Athens two centuries before Gregory of Tours dates his mission to Gaul; the two chronologies cannot both stand, and the atlas records the clash without settling it.
stops.campa: Two philosophers stand at Heliopolis under a sky that is behaving wrongly. The moon crosses the sun out of its season, moves against its own direction, and returns by the road it came. Denis is a pagan still, a young man learned in the courses of the stars, and the one thing his learning cannot supply is a cause. He writes the hour down for Apollophanes and keeps the letter. Seven hundred years later Jacobus de Voragine will set this eclipse at the head of his life of Denis, and the darkness over Judaea will have found its witness.
stops.quote: We were, we twain, at Heliopolis, and we saw the moon of heaven go disordinately, and the time was not convenable.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, tr. William Caxton, rev. F. S. Ellis (Temple Classics, 1900), Life of S. Denis, quoting the epistle to Polycarp and Apollophanes
suggested_refs: The Dionysian corpus letter on the Heliopolis eclipse, source of the Golden Legend's opening scene
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton (Temple Classics, 1900), 'Life of S. Denis', Fordham Medieval Sourcebook

stops.name: Athens, the altar of the unknown God
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Acts 17:34 names Dionysius the Areopagite among Paul's converts; the identification of that man with Denis of Paris is a ninth-century graft by Hilduin and is rejected by modern scholarship.
stops.campa: Paul comes up onto the rock of Ares where the Athenian court sits, and preaches to men who have raised an altar to a god they cannot name. The judge Dionysius questions him about that altar, and the answers do not satisfy a philosopher. He asks for a demonstration instead, and sets the terms himself: a blind man, no incantation, the name of the god and nothing else. The man sees. Dionysius is baptized with his household, and the Areopagus keeps his name for the rest of Christian memory.
stops.quote: If thou say to this blind man in the name of thy God: See, and then he seeth, I shall anon believe in him, but thou shalt use no words of enchantment, for thou mayst haply know some words that have such might and virtue.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, tr. William Caxton, rev. F. S. Ellis (Temple Classics, 1900), Life of S. Denis
suggested_refs: The rock of the Areopagus below the Acropolis, with the bronze plaque of Paul's sermon at its foot
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton (Temple Classics, 1900), 'Life of S. Denis'

stops.name: Athens, the first bishop of the city
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Areopagite, not for Denis of Paris. Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica IV.23.3, quoting Dionysius of Corinth, has the Areopagite as first bishop of Athens. Eusebius does not say he was martyred there; the martyred Athenian bishop of that passage is Publius, succeeded by Quadratus.
stops.campa: Dionysius of Corinth writes to the Athenians and tells them who their first bishop was: the man Paul converted on the hill. Eusebius copies the letter into his history and the record closes there, quietly, with an Athenian in an Athenian see. It is a plain sentence, and it will be the hardest single obstacle to the story Saint-Denis tells about itself. A bishop who governs Athens cannot also be governing the Parisii, in a province he has never seen, in a century that has not begun.
suggested_refs: Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica III.4.11 and IV.23.2-3, on the Athenian succession
sources: Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica IV.23.3, quoting Dionysius of Corinth

stops.name: Rome, seven bishops ordained for Gaul
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, reconstruction for the place. Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum I.30, dates the sending to the consulship of Decius and Gratus, AD 250, but names no sender and never mentions Rome. The commission by Pope Fabian is a later Gallican gloss and is impossible as framed: Fabian died on 20 January 250.
stops.campa: In the consulship of Decius and Gratus seven men are ordained bishops and sent north into Gaul to preach: Catianus for Tours, Trophimus for Arles, Paul for Narbonne, Saturninus for Toulouse, Stremonius for Clermont, Martial for Limoges, and Dionysius for the city of the Parisii. Of the seventh nobody records a birth year, and nobody records a birthplace beyond the word Italia. He is a name attached to a destination. That is the whole of what the earliest witness gives. The rest of the dossier is assembled over the next six centuries.
suggested_refs: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum I.30, the list of the seven bishops sent into Gaul
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum I.30, trans. Ernest Brehaut (1916), Fordham Medieval Sourcebook

stops.name: Ostia, the port no text names
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No ancient source names an embarkation point; the port is supplied by later hagiographic narrative and the absence is recorded in the report as a gap.
stops.campa: The road to Gaul from Rome begins at the mouth of the Tiber, where the grain fleets unload and the sailings west are counted in days. The tradition puts Denis on a ship here because a ship is needed and because Ostia is where Rome keeps them. No text from the period says so. That he left is recorded, and where he sailed from is not recorded anywhere. The harbour is supplied afterwards by hagiographers who could not picture a bishop walking the whole way to the Seine.
suggested_refs: The excavated harbour quarter of Ostia Antica, embarkation point supplied by tradition rather than by any text
sources: General hagiographic reconstruction from later Passio narratives; no ancient text names the port

stops.name: Massilia, the landing on the Provencal coast
stops.date_confidence: local Provencal tradition, absent from Gregory of Tours and possibly borrowed from the Lazarus and Trophimus landing legends of the same coast.
stops.campa: The old Greek harbour of Massilia takes the missionaries ashore, in the account Provence tells. It is the coast where every apostle of Gaul is made to land, Lazarus and Trophimus and the Magdalene among them, and the same few beaches receive them all. Denis steps onto a shore already crowded with arrivals. Gregory of Tours, who names his destination, says nothing whatever about his route, and the entire southern leg of this journey belongs to men who came later and wanted the roads filled in.
suggested_refs: The Vieux-Port of Marseille, landing place shared by most of the apostolic legends of Provence
sources: Provencal local tradition; absent from Gregory of Tours

stops.name: Arelate, the seat of Trophimus
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Hilduin's ninth-century Passio supplies the elaborated itinerary and no corroboration exists outside it.
stops.campa: Of the seven ordained together, Trophimus has the shortest road, and Arles is where he stops. Denis passes through while the amphitheatre still holds games and the forum still holds its magistrates, and the company that left Rome as one body begins to divide along the map. Each bishop peels away toward his own city. This is the last moment at which the mission can be described in the plural, and Hilduin, writing six hundred years afterward, is the only man who describes it at all.
suggested_refs: Hilduin, Passio Sanctorum Dionysii, the elaborated route through Arles
sources: Hilduin, Passio Sanctorum Dionysii (9th c.), elaborated itinerary
Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum I.30

stops.name: Trier, miracles added five centuries later
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a visible inflation. Hilduin extends the itinerary into Germania some five hundred years after the events described; Gregory of Tours has nothing of it.
stops.campa: The Carolingian Passio sends Denis east into Germania, working cures at Trier under the black gate, far off any sane line between Provence and the Seine. The detour costs the story nothing and gains the ninth century a good deal: an abbey whose patron has walked in imperial country. Gregory's Denis goes to Paris and stops. Hilduin's Denis goes wherever the empire of Louis the Pious would like to have been evangelized, and the two itineraries are laid side by side here without a reconciliation.
suggested_refs: Hilduin, Passio Sanctorum Dionysii, the Germania miracles absent from all earlier accounts

stops.name: Meaux, where Sanctinus stays behind
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Local Meaux hagiography names Sanctinus a companion of Denis and first bishop there; companion traditions of this kind are standard padding in later cults seeking apostolic pedigree.
stops.campa: At Meaux on the Marne a companion is dropped from the party and left as the town's first bishop: Sanctinus, whom Meaux will keep and Paris will not dispute. Every diocese within a week's walk of the Seine wants a founder who touched the mission of 250, and the cheapest way to have one is to detach him from Denis on the road. The names multiply as the third century recedes. Rusticus and Eleutherius are attached by the same method, and modern scholarship judges both of them unhistorical.
suggested_refs: The cathedral of Saint-Etienne at Meaux and its claim to Sanctinus as founding bishop
sources: Wikipedia, 'Saint Denis of Paris' (on Rusticus and Eleutherius as non-historical)

stops.name: Ile de la Cite, the church on the island
stops.date_confidence: attested for the see, reconstruction for the founding narrative. Gregory of Tours attests Denis as bishop of the Parisii; the island church and the conversion numbers come from the Catholic Encyclopedia tradition, and the date of 246 sometimes given for the settlement would precede the mission itself.
stops.campa: The Parisii hold an island in the Seine with a bridge at either end, a garrison town of the Roman peace, well placed and thoroughly pagan. Denis builds a church on it and keeps regular services, and the converts come in numbers the tradition likes to call great. This is the one fact about him the earliest witness confirms. Not the tortures, not the walking head, not Athens: only this, that a bishop named Dionysius held the see of Paris. Everything else in the record is built on that sentence.
suggested_refs: The site of the cathedral of Saint-Etienne on the Ile de la Cite, predecessor of Notre-Dame
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum I.30

stops.name: The forum of Lutetia, before the prefect
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Earlier passiones do not name the prefect; Fescenninus Sisinnius appears only from Hilduin onward and the name may be invented.
stops.campa: The pagan priests of Lutetia count the empty temples and go to the governor. Denis is brought up the hill to the forum on the left bank and ordered to sacrifice, and he refuses in the plain formula the law requires him to refuse in, which turns a religious quarrel into a capital case. The governor is called Fescenninus Sisinnius in every retelling from the ninth century forward. No earlier text calls him anything at all, and the atlas keeps the name while noting that it arrives five hundred years late.
suggested_refs: The buried forum of Lutetia under the rue Soufflot, between the boulevard Saint-Michel and the rue Saint-Jacques

stops.name: Saint-Denis-de-la-Chartre, the bread in the cell
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The prison Eucharist is a stock hagiographic motif shared with many martyr narratives of the period, preserved in Hilduin and the Legenda Aurea.
stops.campa: They put him in a cell on the island, and the legend fills it with light. Christ comes in person carrying bread, and Denis says mass there and communes the prisoners around him, so that the sacrament he was arrested for administering is administered to him by its author. A church stands on the spot for centuries under the name Saint-Denis-de-la-Chartre, Denis of the Prison, and is pulled down at last, leaving the story with an address near the rue de la Colombe and no building on it.
stops.quote: Take this, my dear friend, for thy reward is most great with me.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, tr. William Caxton, rev. F. S. Ellis (Temple Classics, 1900), Life of S. Denis, words of Christ appearing to Denis in prison
suggested_refs: The vanished church of Saint-Denis-de-la-Chartre on the Ile de la Cite
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea (13th c.)

stops.name: Arenes de Lutece, the lion that will not touch him
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Legenda Aurea, drawing on Hilduin; a common literary topos across martyr legends rather than a distinct historical event.
stops.campa: He is stripped and put into the amphitheatre with a starved lion, and the crowd on the stone benches gets nothing it came for. The animal will not go near him. The Golden Legend reports the refusal without astonishment, because by the thirteenth century every martyr worth the name has a beast that declines, and the motif travels from life to life like a stage property. The arena is real, cut into the slope above the river, and Paris will bury it for a thousand years and dig it out again in 1869.
suggested_refs: The Arenes de Lutece, rediscovered in 1869 during works on the rue Monge
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea (13th c.), drawing on Hilduin

stops.name: Lutetia, the gridiron, the furnace, the cross
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the particulars. Gregory of Tours says only that Denis suffered various pains for the name of Christ; the gridiron, the furnace, and the crucifixion come from Hilduin and the Legenda Aurea.
stops.campa: They stretch him naked on an iron grill over coals and he sings. They shut him in a furnace and take him out unmarked. They nail him to a cross and he preaches from it. Gregory of Tours, three centuries closer to the man, compresses the whole sequence into four Latin words: various pains for the name of Christ. Everything else here is the ninth century filling a silence it found unbearable, and the atlas keeps the silence and the filling in the same frame.
stops.quote: Lord thy word is vehemently fiery, and thy servant is embraced in the love thereof.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, tr. William Caxton, rev. F. S. Ellis (Temple Classics, 1900), Life of S. Denis, sung by Denis stretched on the gridiron
suggested_refs: Hilduin, Passio Sanctorum Dionysii, source of the ordered sequence of tortures
sources: Gregory of Tours, cited in Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Denis'

stops.name: The Seine at Pont Notre-Dame, a variant drowning
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged, not resolved. A variant local tradition drowns Rusticus and Eleutherius in the Seine rather than beheading them with Denis on the hill; the standard Passio has all three die together.
stops.campa: One strand of the Paris tradition takes the priest and the deacon down to the water instead of up to the hill, weights them, and drowns them in sight of the island where they were arrested. The standard account keeps the three together to the last stroke. Both are told in the same city and neither yields. The names themselves are late: modern scholarship judges Rusticus and Eleutherius unhistorical, which leaves two traditions quarrelling over the deaths of men who may never have lived.
suggested_refs: The Seine bank by the Pont Notre-Dame, site of the minority drowning tradition
sources: Variant local tradition, at odds with the standard Passio account

stops.name: Montmartre, the sword on the mount of Mercury
stops.date_confidence: date not fixed and the sources disagree: c. 250 under Decius, favoured by modern scholarship where Denis's historicity is granted; 258 under Valerian; 270 to 275 in other accounts; and c. 96 under Domitian in the Golden Legend, as a consequence of the Areopagite conflation. The ninth of October is the feast, not an attested day of death. Pin inherited from catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json.
stops.campa: They take him north out of the town to the hill the Romans keep for Mercury and Mars, and there the sword ends it. Rusticus the priest and Eleutherius the deacon die beside him in the account the church will keep. The hill changes its name from the mount of Mars to the mount of the martyrs and holds it. The same imperial machinery of edict and arrest will reach Acacius at Nicomedia half a century later, and both men end in the same Franconian count of fourteen helpers, twelve hundred years after this morning.
stops.quote: the blessed Dionisius, bishop of Paris, after suffering divers pains in Christ's name, ended the present life by the threatening sword.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book I, ch. 30, trans. Ernest Brehaut (1916), Fordham Medieval Sourcebook
suggested_refs: The hill of Montmartre, Mons Martis before the martyrdom and Mons Martyrum after it
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum I.30

stops.name: Saint-Pierre de Montmartre, the rival crypt
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged, not resolved. Two Montmartre sites claim the exact place of beheading, the Chapelle du Martyre on the rue Yvonne-Le-Tac and this crypt, and local tradition supports both.
stops.campa: A second Montmartre tradition puts the block not at the martyrium down the slope but here, under the church of Saint-Pierre, and produces its own stones to prove the point. The hill is small and the two claims stand a few hundred paces apart, close enough that a pilgrim can honour both in one afternoon and never learn which of them is right. Nothing in the written record decides between them, and nothing in the ground has settled it since. The atlas pins the two sites separately and lets them keep the quarrel.
suggested_refs: The crypt of Saint-Pierre de Montmartre, one of the two competing execution sites on the hill

stops.name: The fontaine Saint-Denis, the head washed at the spring
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, devotional. The spring no longer survives identifiably; the coordinate follows the impasse Girardon site on the north slope, against two other values in circulation.
stops.campa: The body stands up, gathers the head into its arms, and starts walking. On the north slope it stops at a spring and washes the face clean of blood, the one domestic gesture in the whole legend, and then goes on north. Later Paris builds over the water and loses it, and later still the guidebooks disagree by four hundred metres about where it ran. The place keeps the name fontaine Saint-Denis long after there is nothing left to drink there. The name outlasts the water by several centuries.
suggested_refs: The site of the fontaine Saint-Denis near the impasse Girardon on the north slope of Montmartre

stops.name: Rue des Martyrs, six kilometres with the head
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. French Wikipedia and the Golden Legend give six kilometres, or two leagues; the six Roman miles sometimes repeated would be about 8.9 km and is an error. Gregory of Tours, three centuries closer, has no cephalophory whatever.
stops.campa: The corridor running north off the hill carries the walk, and carries the name of it still. He preaches the whole way, a sermon of repentance delivered by a man with his mouth in his hands, and an angel goes before him according to the French telling. Six kilometres of road, and at the end of them he chooses his ground and falls. No ancient marker survives along the route. Pilgrims walk it for six hundred years, and the only physical trace left in the city is the name of the street.
stops.quote: the body of S. Denis raised himself up, and bare his head between his arms, as the angel led him two leagues from the place, which is said the hill of the martyrs, unto the place where he now resteth
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, tr. William Caxton, rev. F. S. Ellis (Temple Classics, 1900), Life of S. Denis
suggested_refs: The rue des Martyrs, the surviving toponym of the cephalophore route
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea (13th c.)
Butler's Lives of the Saints (cited, not verified directly)

stops.name: Catulliacus, the widow takes the body
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Catulla and the burial come from the Catholic Encyclopedia tradition and from Hilduin; Gregory of Tours attests only that a basilica dedicated to Denis stood near Paris in his own century.
stops.campa: Where he falls there is a field belonging to a Christian woman named Catulla, who comes out with help, buries the three of them decently, and raises a small shrine over the grave. The estate is called Catulliacus after her, and the village that grows on it will drop her name and take his. Kings will be buried in her field. The first Gothic choir in the world will be built over it. She is given one sentence in the sources, and the ground keeps the rest.
suggested_refs: The site of Catulliacus under the crypt of the basilica of Saint-Denis

stops.name: Saint-Denis, Genevieve builds over the tomb
stops.date_confidence: attested indirectly through the Vita Sanctae Genovefae, composed shortly after 502; no significant discrepancy between the reachable sources on this point.
stops.campa: Two centuries after the burial the shrine is still standing and still visited, and Genevieve of Paris, who held the city through Attila's approach by refusing to let it be evacuated, has a basilica raised over the grave. Her Life records it, and through her Life the atlas gets its first firm date for the site. The cult is older than the building; the building is what makes the cult a place. Every king buried here afterwards is buried on Catulla's field, inside Genevieve's walls.
suggested_refs: The Vita Sanctae Genovefae, composed shortly after 502, earliest witness to the shrine
sources: Vita Sanctae Genovefae, cited in Wikipedia, 'Saint Denis of Paris'

stops.name: Tours, the earliest witness writes him down
stops.date_confidence: attested. Gregory of Tours, writing in the sixth century, is the earliest historical witness to the mission, the see, and the death; the date given is that of Gregory's own death and stands for the closing of his work.
stops.campa: In the see that Catianus took in the same year Denis took Paris, a bishop writes the history of the Franks and gives the martyr of Lutetia four lines. He names the consulship, the seven cities, the office, and the sword. He does not mention Rusticus, or Eleutherius, or Fescenninus Sisinnius, or the lion, or the gridiron, or the head. Everything he omits will be supplied by other men, and the measure of how much was supplied is the distance between these four lines and the Golden Legend.
stops.quote: Beatus Dionysius Parisiorum episcopus diversis pro Christi nomine adfectus poenis praesentem vitam gladio immente finivit.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Liber in Gloria Martyrum, as quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Denis'
suggested_refs: Gregory of Tours, Liber in Gloria Martyrum and Historia Francorum I.30
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum / Liber in Gloria Martyrum, 6th century

stops.name: Saint-Denis, the Passio takes the legend down
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Passio SS. Dionysii Rustici et Eleutherii is dated to about 600 and its attribution to Venantius Fortunatus is disputed; its editors call it legendary, and its place of composition is nowhere fixed beyond Gaul, so the abbey pin is an editorial choice.
stops.campa: Someone in Gaul, perhaps at the abbey and perhaps not, writes the first full life. It gives Denis two companions with Roman names, a governor, an ordered sequence of tortures, and a death, and it is the oldest surviving biography of a man three hundred and fifty years dead. Its own modern editors call it legendary without argument. Every later account descends from it, including the ones read as history for a thousand years, and the atlas records the descent rather than the pedigree.
suggested_refs: The Passio SS. Dionysii Rustici et Eleutherii, c. 600, attribution to Venantius Fortunatus disputed

stops.name: Saint-Denis, Dagobert founds the royal abbey
stops.date_confidence: attested, year disputed. The Gesta Dagoberti and surviving charters support the foundation; the reachable sources give 630, a 628 to 636 window, and 636, while Wikipedia's Basilica of Saint-Denis gives 632, which is adopted. Dagobert rules Austrasia 623 to 634, Neustria and Burgundy 629 to 639, and all the Franks 632 to 639, dying 19 January 639.
stops.campa: Dagobert enlarges the sanctuary over the tomb into a basilica, attaches a community of Benedictines, and endows it richly, and with that act the grave of a third-century missionary becomes an instrument of Frankish kingship. The legend adds a childhood vision of Denis to explain the king's devotion. The charters add land. Clovis, first Catholic king of the Franks, and Clotilde who brought him to the font will end as effigies in this church, whatever the Paris hill they were actually laid in.
suggested_refs: Gesta Dagoberti I Regis Francorum (9th c.), with the surviving foundation charters
sources: Gesta Dagoberti I Regis Francorum (9th c.)

stops.name: Saint-Denis, Fulrad takes the abbacy
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia gives around 749 or 750 for Fulrad's accession as abbot and credits him with the construction of a new church at the abbey.
stops.campa: Fulrad becomes abbot about the year 750 and begins a new church, and for the next thirty years the abbey of a headless bishop is run by one of the most consequential politicians in Europe. He serves the Carolingians as envoy to Rome and gathers relics across the Frankish world. A burial site becomes an institution with a foreign policy. What he builds will be taken down by Suger four centuries later to make room for something the world has not yet seen.
suggested_refs: Fulrad's abbey church at Saint-Denis, replaced by Suger in the twelfth century

stops.name: Saint-Denis, the pope anoints Pepin and his sons
stops.date_confidence: attested; pin and date inherited byte for byte from charlemagne.journey.json, which carries this stop.
stops.campa: Stephen the Second comes over the Alps in person, anoints Pepin the Short king in the abbey church, anoints Charles and Carloman beside him, and forbids the Franks under pain of excommunication ever to take a king from another line. The sacral kingship of the Carolingians is founded on the ground of Denis's grave. That is the moment the martyr stops being a local cult and becomes a piece of the constitution of France. Charlemagne is twelve years old and standing there.
suggested_refs: The anointing of Pepin and his sons at Saint-Denis, 28 July 754

stops.name: Saint-Denis, the bones of Vitus pass through
stops.date_confidence: attested; pin and date inherited from catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json, which dates the translation of Vitus to Saint-Denis to 756 and the onward gift to Corvey afterwards.
stops.campa: Fulrad brings the relics of Vitus of Lucania to the abbey, and for a while two of the fourteen future helpers of Christendom lie under one roof without anyone having thought to count them. The abbey then passes Vitus on to Corvey on the Weser, the first of the fourteen planted in German ground by deliberate policy. Denis stays where he fell. The Franconian shepherd who will assemble the whole company out of a vision in a field is seven hundred years off.
suggested_refs: The translation of Vitus from Saint-Denis to the imperial abbey of Corvey

stops.name: Saint-Denis, Pepin buried face down at the door
stops.date_confidence: attested; pin and date inherited byte for byte from charlemagne.journey.json.
stops.campa: Pepin dies and is buried at his own order face down in the threshold of the church, so that everyone entering the abbey walks over the king. He gives penance as the reason. His sons divide the kingdom above his back, and Charlemagne takes the western half of it. The martyr's church now holds the founder of a dynasty in its doorway, and the pattern is set for a thousand years: the kings of the Franks and then of France come here to be anointed, and they come back here to be buried.
suggested_refs: The threshold burial of Pepin the Short at Saint-Denis, September 768

stops.name: Saint-Denis, Charlemagne at the rededication
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 775 by the Carolingian annals; the day given is the traditional date of the dedication and is not independently confirmed here.
stops.campa: The king who was anointed here as a boy comes back to see Fulrad's church consecrated, and the abbey receives its emperor. Charlemagne will grant it privileges, immunities, and its own markets, and the monks will remember him as a founder second only to Dagobert. Denis has been dead five centuries by now and has acquired, in place of a biography, a clientele: a dynasty, an abbot, a treasury, a fair, and a road north out of Paris that men walk on purpose in October.
suggested_refs: The Carolingian annals on the rededication of the abbey church, 775
sources: Carolingian annals, cited in the geography lens

stops.name: Saint-Denis, a Greek codex arrives from Byzantium
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia, 'Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite': Michael the Second sends the manuscript to Louis the Pious in 827 and Louis donates it to the abbey.
stops.campa: The emperor Michael in Constantinople sends Louis the Pious a diplomatic gift: a Greek manuscript of the works of one Dionysius the Areopagite, the celestial hierarchies, the divine names, the mystical theology. Louis gives it to the abbey of Saint-Denis, where nobody can read it and everybody can read the name on it. The confusion that will hold France for a thousand years enters the country as a present, unopened, in a language the recipients do not have.
suggested_refs: The Greek codex of the Corpus Areopagiticum given by Michael the Second, 827

stops.name: Saint-Denis, Hilduin makes the three men one
stops.date_confidence: attested. Louis the Pious commissions the biography in 835 (Wikipedia, 'Hilduin of Saint-Denis'); the Rescriptum, also called the Areopagitica, dates to about 835 to 836, and the separate Passio sanctissimi Dionysii to 835 to 840. The two works are routinely conflated and are kept apart here.
stops.campa: Hilduin, abbot of the house that owns both the grave and the codex, is commissioned by the emperor to write his patron's life, and he writes it with the manuscript open. The Athenian judge of Acts, the author of the Greek treatises, and the bishop beheaded on Montmartre become one man: Paul's convert, philosopher of the angelic orders, missionary to Gaul, martyr of the Parisii. The abbey now owns the philosophy as well as the bones, and the correction will take until 1969.
suggested_refs: Hilduin, Rescriptum (Areopagitica), c. 835-836, and Passio sanctissimi Dionysii, 835-840

stops.name: Saint-Denis, Eriugena makes the Greek speak Latin
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia dates Hilduin's own version to about 838 and judges it almost unintelligible; Eriugena completes his translation in 862 at the request of Charles the Bald, and it is criticized for excessive literalness.
stops.campa: Hilduin's Latin of the Greek is judged almost unintelligible, so Charles the Bald sets John Scotus Eriugena to it, and by 862 the West has a readable Pseudo-Dionysius. It circulates in few copies and is faulted for following the Greek word by word. From it descend John Sarrazin's commentary of 1140 and translation of 1165, Grosseteste's version of the 1240s, and the standard Paris compilation of the thirteenth century. The mystical theology of the Latin Middle Ages enters through a Parisian martyr's supposed authorship.
suggested_refs: Eriugena's Latin translation of the Corpus Areopagiticum, 862, made for Charles the Bald

stops.name: Regensburg, Saint Emmeram claims the body
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The abbey documents a Saint Denis altar and a stone relief of about 1052, consistent with the eleventh-century Regensburg claim to hold Denis's body; the ninth-century translation asserted in circulation is unsupported by the reachable article and is recorded as a gap.
stops.campa: The Bavarian abbey of Saint Emmeram announces that it has the body of Saint Denis, obtained out of Francia, and cuts a relief of him in stone to make the point permanent. Saint-Denis, which has the grave, the kings, and the abbot, disputes it furiously. Relics are a currency, and a disputed body is a dispute about pilgrim traffic and the money it brings. The Regensburg altar stands regardless, and two houses in two countries go on holding the same saint.
suggested_refs: The Saint Denis altar and the c. 1052 stone relief at St Emmeram's Abbey, Regensburg

stops.name: Saint-Denis, Abelard says it is not the same man
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia records Abelard's public challenge to the identification while a monk of the abbey, and the community's hostility to it.
stops.campa: Pierre Abelard, in residence at the abbey and reading Bede, points out that the Areopagite was bishop of Athens and that the man in the crypt was not, and he says it where the monks can hear him. They react as a house reacts when a lodger questions its title deeds. He is threatened, and he leaves. He is right, and it changes nothing for eight hundred years: the abbey keeps the identification, the kings keep the abbey, and the correction waits for Koch and Stiglmayr in 1895.
suggested_refs: Abelard's dispute with the monks of Saint-Denis over the identity of their patron, c. 1121

stops.name: Montmartre, Louis the Sixth builds the Martyrium
stops.date_confidence: attested for the twelfth century by Wikipedia, 'Montmartre'; the precise year within the reign of Louis the Sixth, 1108 to 1137, is not fixed by the reachable sources. Coordinate corrected to the geocode of 11 rue Yvonne-Le-Tac.
stops.campa: The king builds a chapel on the spot where the sword is said to have fallen, and the hill acquires a destination. Pilgrims climb out of the city to the Martyrium and then take the road north to the abbey, walking the saint's own last journey in the right order and the right direction. A priory follows on the site, the abbaye d'en bas, occupied by nuns from 1686. Montmartre keeps the death, Saint-Denis keeps the body, and the six kilometres between them are walked for six hundred years.
suggested_refs: The Martyrium chapel of Louis the Sixth at Montmartre, ancestor of the present crypt on the rue Yvonne-Le-Tac

stops.name: Saint-Denis, Suger dedicates the first Gothic choir
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia, 'Basilica of Saint-Denis': Suger begins rebuilding in 1135 and the new choir is finished and dedicated on 11 June 1144 in the presence of the king, when the relics are installed beneath the new high altar. The date of 1140 sometimes given for the translation belongs to the works, not the dedication.
stops.campa: Suger takes down Fulrad's church and puts up something without precedent: pointed arches carrying the weight outward, walls opened into coloured glass, a choir built to be full of light because the treatises attributed to the patron say that God is light and that the mind climbs to him by material things. The relics go under the new high altar on the day of the dedication, with the king present. At one of its altars Suger records the first European relics of Eustace, another of the fourteen.
suggested_refs: Suger, De Administratione and De Consecratione, on the choir dedicated 11 June 1144
sources: Suger, De Administratione and De Consecratione

stops.name: Saint-Denis, Joan of Arc lays down her armour
stops.date_confidence: attested; pin and date inherited byte for byte from joan_of_arc.journey.json, which carries this stop with the same coordinate.
stops.campa: Joan of Arc holds the abbey town through the failed assault on Paris, skirmishing daily from the Porte Saint-Honore toward Montmartre, and before she is led south she hangs her white armour and a sword as an offering before the image of Our Lady in the church. She leaves her war in the martyr's keeping. The cry the kings of France carry into battle is his name, Montjoie Saint-Denis, and the girl who put a king back on the throne ends her campaign at his tomb.
suggested_refs: The ex-voto of Joan's white armour before Our Lady at the basilica of Saint-Denis, September 1429

stops.name: Regensburg, the count closes at fourteen
stops.date_confidence: attested for the closed list by about 1500 through catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json, which locates it across Regensburg, Bamberg, Wurzburg and Nuremberg. The date of 1350 sometimes given for Denis's entry into the group rests on the general tradition of the cult and is a reconstruction.
stops.campa: Across Regensburg, Bamberg, Wurzburg and Nuremberg the helpers settle into a fixed sequence: Acacius, Barbara, Blaise, Catherine, Christopher, Cyriacus, Denis, Erasmus, Eustace, George, Giles, Margaret, Pantaleon, Vitus. Each takes an affliction. Denis takes headache, which is the kind of joke the late Middle Ages made in earnest. The bishop of Paris and patron of a kingdom enters a Franconian devotion as a specialist, and the abbey on the Seine has no say in the matter.
suggested_refs: The closed Franconian list of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, c. 1500

stops.name: Montmartre, the abbey pulled down
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia, 'Montmartre', dates the demolition of the abbey to 1790; the figure of 1794 in circulation is the year the last abbess was guillotined, not the year of the demolition.
stops.campa: The Revolution suppresses the house on the hill and takes the buildings down. The last abbess, blind and deaf and past seventy, goes to the guillotine four years after that, and the confusion of the two dates outlives both of them. The Martyrium is unroofed and the site passes into private hands. For sixty-five years the most precise address in the whole legend of Saint Denis is a plot of ground in a quarry district with nothing standing on it to say what happened there.
suggested_refs: The demolished abbey of Montmartre and the fate of its last abbess

stops.name: Saint-Denis, the kings taken out of the ground
stops.date_confidence: attested for August and October 1793 by Wikipedia, 'Basilica of Saint-Denis', following the decrees of the Convention and the records of Alexandre Lenoir; the specific day given stands for the August campaign and is not itself attested.
stops.campa: By decree the tombs are opened and the kings and queens of France are lifted out, from the Merovingians to the last Bourbon, and thrown into two pits in the abbey grounds with quicklime. Alexandre Lenoir carries off what sculpture he can save. The effigy of Clovis survives and the bodies do not. A necropolis grown around a martyr's grave is emptied in ten weeks, and the relics of Denis are already gone, taken into a Paris parish church by men who preferred them hidden to burned.
suggested_refs: The Convention decrees of 1793 and the records of Alexandre Lenoir on the emptying of the royal tombs
sources: Contemporary Convention decrees; records of Alexandre Lenoir

stops.name: Saint-Denis, the ossuary and the relics come back
stops.date_confidence: attested. Restoration-era administrative records of the basilica for the 1817 ossuary; Wikipedia, 'Basilica of Saint-Denis', for the return of the relics of Denis in 1819 and for the nineteenth-century restorations.
stops.campa: Louis the Eighteenth has the royal bones dug back out of the pits, unidentifiable and mixed, and laid together in one ossuary in the crypt: a dynasty reduced to a single box because nobody can tell one king from another. Two years afterwards the relics of Denis come home from the parish church that sheltered them. Francois Debret begins the restoration and makes a wreck of parts of it, and Viollet-le-Duc spends much of the rest of the century undoing his work.
suggested_refs: The Bourbon ossuary in the crypt of Saint-Denis, assembled 1817
sources: Restoration-era administrative records of the basilica

stops.name: Montmartre, the oratory over the martyrdom
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia, 'Montmartre': an oratory is built at 11 rue Yvonne-Le-Tac in 1855 and renovated in 1994. Coordinate corrected to the geocode of that address.
stops.campa: An oratory is built at 11 rue Yvonne-Le-Tac over the old Martyrium, and the cult resumes at the address it lost in 1790. It is renovated in 1994 and called now the Crypte du martyrium de saint Denis, a low vaulted room off a narrow street, open to whoever rings the bell at the door. Above it the hill is filling with painters and windmills and cabarets, and the crowds going up to them pass the oldest address in the story of the city's first bishop without stopping.
suggested_refs: The Crypte du martyrium de saint Denis, 11 rue Yvonne-Le-Tac, Paris

stops.name: Montmartre, the white basilica and Merson's apse
stops.date_confidence: attested for the construction span 1876 to 1919 by Wikipedia, 'Montmartre'; the day given is the laying of the foundation stone, and Merson's apse mosaic is executed in the following decades. Pin inherited from catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json.
stops.campa: France builds Sacre-Coeur on the summit as a national vow after the defeat of 1870, and its travertine goes white in the rain. Luc-Olivier Merson designs the apse mosaic, the largest in the country, and sets Christ over a hill that has been a place of execution since Mercury had a temple on it. The basilica is not raised for Denis and it stands on his ground all the same, borrowing a martyr it does not name. From the steps a visitor can see the whole six kilometres of the walk laid out to the north.
suggested_refs: The apse mosaic of Sacre-Coeur, designed by Luc-Olivier Merson

stops.name: Vatican City, the calendar separates the two Dionysii
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1969 reform of the General Roman Calendar under Paul VI, which formally separates Denis of Paris from Dionysius the Areopagite. Scholarship had settled the question earlier, with Koch and Stiglmayr in 1895.
stops.campa: The revised Roman Calendar takes the Athenian judge, the Greek theologian, and the bishop of Paris, and gives them back their separate lives. Denis keeps the ninth of October with Rusticus and Eleutherius, the day Pius the Fifth had carried into the Tridentine calendar of 1568, and loses the philosophy. It is a retraction eleven hundred years after the error and seventy-four years after the proof of it, issued quietly, by an institution that does not often print corrections.
suggested_refs: Calendarium Romanum, 1969 reform under Paul VI
sources: Calendarium Romanum, 1969 reform under Paul VI

stops.name: Saint-Denis, the church measured to the millimetre
stops.date_confidence: attested for the posthumous publication of Sumner McKnight Crosby's The Royal Abbey of Saint-Denis in 1987; the reachable source does not say whether his fieldwork located or verified an original grave, and that is recorded as a gap.
stops.campa: An American art historian spends a career photographing and measuring the abbey stone by stone, and the monograph appears after his death with the dimensions of Suger's choir fixed to a precision the twelfth century never had for itself. The building is now known better than the man under it. Nothing in the reachable record says whether anyone has ever found the grave of the bishop that this whole apparatus of kings and glass and translation was raised over.
suggested_refs: Sumner McKnight Crosby, The Royal Abbey of Saint-Denis (posthumous, 1987)
